newsitem.title: UK: UK's FTSE 100 seen stagnating in second half.
newsitem.headline: UK's FTSE 100 seen stagnating in second half.

text.p: A two-year old bull run in UK equities may run out of steam in the second half of 1997, as the prospect of rising interest rates weighs on sentiment, analysts said.

Questioned in a Reuters survey earlier this month, 12 banks and brokerages on average forecast the FTSE 100 to end the year at 4,725, not far from its June 27 close of 4,640.3 and below its record finish of 4,783.1 set on June 13.
Forecasts were in a wide range between 4,000 and 5,000. Expectations for the end of 1998 were scarcely more optimistic. The median of eight forecasts saw the FTSE 100 just 225 points higher at 4,950.

After hitting a succession of record highs in the first six months of the year, the threat of rising domestic interest rates and slower company profit growth would both contribute to an expected stagnation in the equity market, analysts said.
Yet events in the next few days could determine the market's direction through the next six months, market participants said.

"People are just waiting for Wednesday's Budget to see what sort of economic environment we will have going forward," said David Bruce, director of Abbey Life Investment Services, which controls funds totalling some eight billion stg.
One specific fear for the UK equity market is that the Budget would scale back tax breaks for pension funds that boost the value of equity dividends.
Yet a more general fear is that it would not do enough in terms of tax increases to cool the strength of consumer demand and prevent the economy overheating.
A trend towards rising interest rates elsewhere in the developed world could also create a less benign backdrop for the UK market.

"The stock market will trade sideways over the next few months. The environment won't be friendly as we enter the late stage of the (economic) cycle," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust.
Shares may have to wait until the second half of 1998 to regain their upward momentum, strategists said.

"Equities will be reassured by the policy response (of higher interest rates) which will have an impact reasonably quickly in terms of lower inflation and an easier monetary policy," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse Tilney.
For much of the first half of the year, shares in London were overshadowed by the prospect of an election and the likely return of the first Labour party government in 18 years.

In the event, the FTSE 100 shot to record levels in the wake of the May 1 election, as the duly-elected Labour administration enhanced its market credibility by giving the Bank of England freedom to set interest rates to control inflation.
Over the first half, the FTSE 100 rose some 500 points or 12 percent. But the index still underperformed other leading indexes such as the U.S. Dow and Germany's Dax.
UK market watchers pointed out that the gains of the first half of the year were heavily concentrated in a small number of sectors, particularly the banks.
They said others may have to take up the running if the upward momentum was to be continued.

Outside the charmed circle of the leading bank, drug and oil stocks, companies have found the going tough -- one reason the FTSE 250 index of mid-range stocks has lately dropped to its lowest point since December 1996.
Andy Hartwill, strategist at SocGen, predicted the FTSE 100 will end the year at around 4,600, partly because he expects the financial sector to lose its sparkle.

"In the short term there is a possibility of a post-Budget relief rally," Hartwill said, "but the economic backdrop is not that great and we are sticking with our 4,600 year-end target... I think we have seen the best of it."
